title: Aamir Khan Is Producing a Sunny Deol Film. Twenty-Five Years After Gadar vs Lagaan, Bollywood's Greatest Rivalry Becomes Its Most Epic Collaboration.
excerpt: Batwara 1947, a Partition drama directed by Rajkumar Santoshi with A.R. Rahman's score, Santosh Sivan's camera, and Preity Zinta's first lead role in eight years, arrives August 14. The timing is poetic.
body:
In 2001, two Bollywood titans went to war at the box office. On one side, Sunny Deol in Gadar: Ek Prem Katha, roaring and pulling out hand pumps and making the entire country choose a side. On the other, Aamir Khan in Lagaan, quietly building the greatest underdog sports film India had ever seen. Both films became massive hits. The rivalry became folklore.

In 2026, Aamir Khan is producing Sunny Deol's next film.

Let that sink in.

The Film

Batwara 1947 — formerly known as Lahore 1947, retitled to sidestep geopolitical sensitivities — is a Partition drama adapted from Asghar Wajahat's acclaimed 1989 play Jis Lahore Nai Vekhya, O Jamya E Nai. Directed by Rajkumar Santoshi, with music by A.R. Rahman and lyrics by Javed Akhtar, the film releases theatrically on August 14, 2026 — Independence Day weekend. The symbolism writes itself.

Sunny Deol unveiled the first-look motion poster on June 9, and it's exactly the kind of image that stops you mid-scroll. Deol stands at the center, torch blazing, with Preity Zinta and Karan Deol beside him as flames consume the background. "In times of hatred and fear, he chose courage," reads the tagline. Another frame shows him sprinting alongside a steam train through a landscape of destruction — primal, elemental, classic Sunny Deol, but in a register that feels more Gadar than Border.

The cast runs deep: Shabana Azmi, Ali Fazal, and Abhimanyu Singh fill out the ensemble. Cinematography is by Santosh Sivan, which alone guarantees that whatever unfolds on screen will look like a painting on fire.

The Reunion Nobody Saw Coming

The Sunny-Santoshi reunion is the headline, and it should be. The director gave Deol three of his most iconic performances — Ghayal (1990), Damini (1993), and Ghatak (1996). That last one was nearly 30 years ago. In the years between, Santoshi made occasional films and Deol rode a rollercoaster of hits and misses. But when these two are together, something clicks — a specific kind of righteous, burning intensity that nobody else in Hindi cinema quite replicates.

And then there's the Aamir factor. These are two men who've competed at the box office at least four times:

  • 1990: Ghayal vs Dil
  • 1996: Ghatak vs Raja Hindustani
  • 2001: Gadar vs Lagaan

Every single time, both films succeeded. There was never a loser — just two very different approaches to stardom that somehow coexisted. Now, exactly 25 years after the greatest Bollywood box-office clash in history, they're on the same side. The fact that Lagaan is literally re-releasing in theaters this same week while Batwara 1947 builds its campaign feels like the universe writing fan fiction.

Preity Zinta's Second Act

Buried in the Batwara announcement is a comeback that deserves its own spotlight. Preity Zinta's last Hindi film was Bhaiaji Superhit! in 2018 — a forgettable comedy that did nothing for her legacy. Before that, she was one of the defining faces of early-2000s Bollywood: Dil Chahta Hai, Kal Ho Naa Ho, Veer-Zaara, Lakshya. She didn't just play the love interest; she played women with opinions and spines and the kind of smile that made you believe things would work out.

Zinta has called Batwara 1947 the toughest film of her career. Given the Partition subject matter, the emotional weight, and the scale of production, that checks out. She also has Kunal Kemmu's dark comedy Vibe arriving September 18, making this something of a full-blown second act — not a cameo return, but a real one.

What the Diaspora Should Know

The Partition of 1947 is not a distant historical event for the Indian diaspora. It's family lore, whispered stories from grandparents, the reason certain aunties get quiet at dinner. A film that treats the subject with the weight of Wajahat's source material and the craft of Rahman, Akhtar, Sivan, and Santoshi has real potential to become a communal experience — the kind of film you go see with your parents on a Saturday afternoon and then sit in the parking lot talking about for an hour.

August 14 is a long way out, but the motion poster has already done its job. The train. The fire. The torch. And at the center, Sunny Deol — older, broader, still carrying that unshakeable conviction that has defined his best work.

This time, Aamir Khan is standing behind the camera. Making sure the world sees it.
